MassTool: A Multi-Task Search-Based Tool Retrieval Framework for Large Language Models

Jianghao Lin Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Email: chiangel@sjtu.edu.cn    Xinyuan Wang Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Email: wnzhang@sjtu.edu.cn    Xinyi Dai Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab    Menghui Zhu Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab    Bo Chen Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab    Ruiming Tang Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab    Yong Yu Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University    Weinan Zhang Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract

Tool retrieval is a critical component in enabling large language models (LLMs) to interact effectively with external tools. It aims to precisely filter the massive tools into a small set of candidates for the downstream tool-augmented LLMs. However, most existing approaches primarily focus on optimizing tool representations, often neglecting the importance of precise query comprehension. To address this gap, we introduce MassTool, a multi-task search-based framework designed to enhance both query representation and tool retrieval accuracy. MassTool employs a two-tower architecture: a tool usage detection tower that predicts the need for function calls, and a tool retrieval tower that leverages a query-centric graph convolution network (QC-GCN) for effective query-tool matching. It also incorporates search-based user intent modeling (SUIM) to handle diverse and out-of-distribution queries, alongside an adaptive knowledge transfer (AdaKT) module for efficient multi-task learning. By jointly optimizing tool usage detection loss, list-wise retrieval loss, and contrastive regularization loss, MassTool establishes a robust dual-step sequential decision-making pipeline for precise query understanding. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in improving retrieval accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/wxydada/MassTool.

1 Introduction

Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have significantly improved their abilities in tasks like mathematical reasoning [35, 23] and natural dialogues [38, 12]. However, these models are inherently limited by their fixed parameters and static context windows [28], requiring continuous retraining to keep pace with rapidly evolving real-world knowledge. Tool learning [15, 27, 31, 36] offers a promising solution by allowing LLMs to dynamically access external tools. This approach enables real-time data access and complex computation, significantly enhancing LLM performance in real-world applications. However, most previous research [18, 37, 19] on tool integration primarily focuses on a small, well-defined set of APIs11 1 In this paper, the term “tool” is interchangeable with “function” and “API”.. Such a formulation neglects the fact that real-world web-scale applications involve a massive number of candidate tools as it is impractical to take descriptions of all tools as the input for LLMs due to context limitations and computational constraints. As shown in Figure 1(a), it is essential to develop efficient tool retrieval mechanisms that can quickly filter these massive tool pools into a manageable set of candidates.

Most existing tool retrieval methods leverage dense retrieval techniques [5, 30, 48] to measure semantic similarities between user queries and tool descriptions. While these approaches have advanced tool representations, e.g., capturing set-wise tool correlation [32], applying multi-stage refinement [51, 25], and modeling diverse use cases [49], they often overlook the importance of precise query representation, which is critical for accurately capturing diverse user intents. Although related work in web search [17, 29, 16] has extensively explored query understanding, the same level of attention has not been given to user intent modeling in tool retrieval. Previous studies [2, 9, 10, 43] have made initial attempts at query optimization but still face two major challenges:

First, tool retrieval naturally involves a dual-step sequential decision-making process. As illustrated in Figure 1(b), this process requires determining whether a given query actually needs a tool invocation (i.e., tool usage detection) before retrieving a set of suitable tools (i.e., tool retrieval). Many queries can be handled directly by LLMs without external tools, e.g., chit-chat, text summarization, and general knowledge responses. However, existing research on tool retrieval usually overlooks the crucial preliminary step and assumes that all training queries are tool-dependent, which can lead to suboptimal performance, as it causes a biased view of the input queries and global user intents.

Secondly, user queries often exhibit significant out-of-distribution (OOD) variation, with diverse and overlapping intents expressed in varying forms. As shown in Figure 1(c), even when targeting similar intents, such as stock market information, the phrasing of these queries can differ greatly due to factors like regional dialects and cultural nuances [13]. This diversity poses a major challenge for effective intent modeling, especially in tool retrieval, since the retriever is often a smaller language model (e.g., BERT-base with 110M parameters) to ensure lightweight integration with downstream LLMs.

To address these challenges, we introduce MassTool, a multi-task search-based tool retrieval framework designed to optimize query representation under a joint modeling of both tool usage detection and tool retrieval tasks with a two-tower architecture. The tool usage detection tower predicts the probability that a query requires external tools and injects the hidden states as detective knowledge to the tool retrieval tower. The tool retrieval tower includes a query-centric graph convolution network (QC-GCN) to capture collaborative query-tool patterns, a search-based user intent modeling (SUIM) module for handling diverse and OOD queries by integrating semantically relevant neighbors with a dynamic filtering mechanism, and an adaptive knowledge transfer (AdaKT) module for integrating knowledge across the two towers. Finally, we fuse the enhanced query representations for query-tool matching score estimation. In this way, we establish a dual-step sequential decision-making pipeline to optimize query representations for precise tool retrieval.

Moreover, for the preliminary step of tool usage detection, we construct a new tool usage detection dataset (ToolDet) with 31,229 non-tool-invocation queries. This dataset is built by filtering the Chatbot Arena dataset [50] and validated by human annotators and LLMs. Our tool usage detection dataset is dataset-agnostic and can serve as an auxiliary resource for existing tool retrieval datasets.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

  • •

    We are the first to introduce the multi-task modeling paradigm in tool retrieval for large language models, integrating both tool usage detection and tool retrieval to improve query understanding.

  • •

    We introduce MassTool, a two-tower architecture featuring three core modules for query representation optimization: QC-GCN for collaborative query-tool pattern learning, SUIM for handling diverse and OOD queries, and AdaKT for cross-task knowledge fusion.

  • •

    We release the first dataset for tool usage detection (i.e., ToolDet) consisting of queries that do not require tool invocations, enabling multi-task training for improved retrieval performance. The dataset is open-sourced to support future research.

  • •

    Extensive experiments on three public datasets validate the superiority of our proposed MassTool for query comprehension and tool retrieval, compared with existing baseline methods.

2 Related Work

Tool-Augmented Large Language Models.

Integrating external tools with large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a key direction for enhancing their capabilities in complex tasks [31, 27]. Existing approaches can be broadly classified into tuning-free and tuning-based methods. Tuning-free methods [21, 37, 47] rely on in-context learning with prompt engineering techniques, such as chain-of-thought [44] prompting and demonstration ordering [20], to guide LLMs in complex reasoning [21, 37, 47]. Tuning-based methods [5, 30, 36, 40, 46, 19] directly finetune LLMs on specialized tool datasets, significantly enhancing their function-calling abilities through supervised training. Real-world applications require LLMs to handle thousands of potential tools across diverse domains. Given context and latency constraints, the visible candidate set is typically small, highlighting the need for efficient tool retrieval to filter these vast tool pools into a manageable set [18, 19, 22].

Tool Retrieval.

Tool retrieval is critical for identifying relevant tools from large repositories in response to user queries. Methods generally fall into two categories: term-based and semantic-based approaches. Term-based methods, like TF-IDF [39] and BM25 [34], rely on sparse lexical matching, while semantic-based methods leverage dense representations to capture deeper query-tool relationships, like ANCE [45], TAS-B [8], coCondensor [4], and Contriever [11]. Recent work has focused on adapting deep semantic models specifically for tool retrieval, incorporating task-specific architectures and training strategies to improve relevance ranking [51, 26, 25, 49, 32, 3]. For example, COLT [32] conducts scene-aware collaborative learning for better tool representations and proposes a new metric to assess the tool retrieval performance based on completeness.

3 Problem Formulation

Suppose that we have a global tool set 𝒯={(ti,di)}i=1T\mathcal{T}=\{(t_{i},d_{i})\}_{i=1}^{T}, where the ii-th tool tit_{i} is associated with its description did_{i}. Each instance of the tool retrieval dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} can be formulated as a triplet (q,y,𝒯q)(q,y,\mathcal{T}_{q}), where qq is the query, y∈{1,0}y\in\{1,0\} is the tool usage label indicating whether the query needs tool invocation or not, and 𝒯q\mathcal{T}_{q} is the golden tool set required by the query qq. If query qq does not require tool invocation (i.e., y=0y=0), the golden tool set would be empty (i.e., 𝒯q=∅\mathcal{T}_{q}=\varnothing). Therefore, the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} can be divided into two subsets:

𝒟\displaystyle\mathcal{D} =𝒟d​e​t∪𝒟r​e​t,\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{det}\cup\mathcal{D}_{ret}, (1)
𝒟d​e​t\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{det} ={(q,y,𝒯q)∈𝒟|y=0,𝒯q=∅},\displaystyle=\{(q,y,\mathcal{T}_{q})\in\mathcal{D}\;|\;y=0,\mathcal{T}_{q}=\varnothing\},
𝒟r​e​t\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{ret} ={(q,y,𝒯q)∈𝒟|y=1,𝒯q≠∅}.\displaystyle=\{(q,y,\mathcal{T}_{q})\in\mathcal{D}\;|\;y=1,\mathcal{T}_{q}\neq\varnothing\}.

Next, we can define the tool retrieval task in our paper as a dual-step sequential decision-making problem. That is, given the user query qq, our goal is to perform the following two tasks:

  • •

    Tool Usage Detection. We should first predict whether query qq truly needs tool invocation for tool-augmented LLMs or not, i.e., the tool usage label yy.

  • •

    Tool Retrieval. If the tool usage label is predicted as positive, we should then retrieve the top-KK most suitable tools from the global tool pool, i.e., the golden tool set 𝒯q⊂𝒯\mathcal{T}_{q}\subset\mathcal{T}.

It is worth noting that previous works on tool retrieval generally assume that all the queries are tool-dependent, i.e., the dataset they use is merely 𝒟r​e​t\mathcal{D}_{ret} in Eq. 1. In contrast, we are the first to formulate the tool retrieval task as a dual-step sequential decision-making problem, and further extend the dataset 𝒟r​e​t\mathcal{D}_{ret} with 𝒟d​e​t\mathcal{D}_{det}. In this way, we can conduct the multi-task joint modeling, and incorporate the information gain between the two predictive stages to further enhance the retrieval performance.

4 Methodology

As shown in Figure 2, we formulate a dual-step sequential decision-making problem, and perform a joint modeling of both tool usage detection and tool retrieval. The MassTool framework follows the two-tower architecture consisting of (a) tool usage detection tower, and (b) tool retrieval tower.

4.1 Tool Usage Detection

The tool usage detection tower focuses on determining whether tool invocation is required for a given query. As shown in Figure 2, we input the query q∈𝒟q\in\mathcal{D} through the pretrained language model (PLM) and projection layer to obtain the detective knowledge hh. The projection is a linear layer with ReLU activation [1]. The detective knowledge hh encodes the semantic and contextual features essential for tool usage detection, and is then fed into the final prediction layer for tool usage probability estimation, followed by binary cross-entropy loss:

y^=σ⁡(Linear⁡(h))∈(0,1),\hat{y}=\sigma\left(\operatorname{Linear}(h)\right)\in(0,1), (2)
ℒd​e​t=y​log⁡y^+(1−y)​log⁡(1−y^),\mathcal{L}_{det}=y\log\hat{y}+(1-y)\log(1-\hat{y}), (3)

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, and y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} is the label. Moreover, the detective knowledge hh will be passed to the adaptive knowledge transfer module in the tool retrieval tower.

4.2 Tool Retrieval

The tool retrieval aims to estimate the matching score between the query qq and each tool tt from the global tool set 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Then, we can sort the tools based on the estimated scores and select the top-ranked ones for downstream LLMs. As shown in Figure 2, the tool retrieval tower comprises three core components: query-centric graph convolution network (QC-GCN), search-based user intent modeling (SUIM), and adaptive knowledge transfer module (AdaKT).

4.2.1 Query-Centric Graph Convolution Network (QC-GCN)

To better model the relational knowledge between queries and tools, as well as the contextual information for application scenes, we regard the queries and tools as nodes, and construct the following two bipartite graphs with a centric view towards the queries:

  • •

    The query-tool graph links a query qq to each tool tt in its golden tool set 𝒯q\mathcal{T}_{q}. The golden-tool linkages for different queries can overlap with each other, thereby conveying the contextual connections and collaborative patterns among queries and tools.

  • •

    The query-scene graph is built to represent the global patterns by defining the golden tool set 𝒯q\mathcal{T}_{q} for a given query as a unified scene ss, following previous work [32]. The tools in one golden tool set 𝒯q\mathcal{T}_{q} are jointly required to fully address one user request. For example, to make a travel plan for the user, LLMs have to incorporate tools like weather forecasts, hotel booking, restaurant reservations, etc. The joint modeling of scene-level information can help capture the intent-level correlation, and deepen the insights for user query understanding.

After constructing the two bipartite graphs, we apply a query-centric graph convolution network using LightGCN [7] to capture high-order collaborative signals among queries, tools, and scenes, resulting in final representations for the query-tool graph: eqQ​Te_{q}^{QT} and etQ​Te_{t}^{QT}, where QT stands for query-tool graph. Due to the page limitation, details about lightGCN can be found in Appendix B.1. We can conduct similar operations on the query-scene graph, resulting in representations eqQ​Se_{q}^{QS} and esQ​Se_{s}^{QS}. Finally, we calculate the graph-enhanced representations for query qq and tool tt:

eqg​r​a​p​h=eqQ​T+eqQ​S,etg​r​a​p​h=etQ​T.e_{q}^{graph}=e_{q}^{QT}+e_{q}^{QS},\;\;e_{t}^{graph}=e_{t}^{QT}. (4)

As shown in Figure 2, the tool representation etg​r​a​p​he_{t}^{graph} is preserved for the final matching score estimation, and the query representation eqg​r​a​p​he_{q}^{graph} would be further enhanced via the search-based user intent modeling and adaptive knowledge transfer module.

4.2.2 Search-based User Intent Modeling (SUIM)

The user queries are often out-of-distribution (OOD) with diverse and overlapping intents in varying forms, making it difficult to directly match them to the correct tools. To this end, as shown in Figure 2, we propose search-based user intent modeling to further enrich the query representation based on its semantically nearest neighbor queries.

To be specific, we maintain a global query pool based on the retrieval training dataset 𝒬={q|(q,y,𝒯q)∈𝒟r​e​t}\mathcal{Q}=\{q|(q,y,\mathcal{T}_{q})\in\mathcal{D}_{ret}\}. Then, we first conduct semantic search to retrieve the top-KK semantically relevant queries based on cosine similarity. By sorting the cosine similarity, we can get the top-KK nearest neighbor set 𝒩qK\mathcal{N}_{q}^{K} for the target query qq.

While semantic search retrieves the most relevant neighbors with potentially similar user intents, some rare or unconventional queries may still result in the retrieval of irrelevant neighbors. To address this, we apply dynamic filtering to filter the top-KK neighbor set 𝒩qK\mathcal{N}_{q}^{K} with a hyperparameter threshold ϵ\epsilon, resulting in the final neighbor set 𝒩qd​y​n={q′|sc​o​s(q,q′)>ϵ,q′∈𝒩qK}.\mathcal{N}_{q}^{dyn}=\left\{q^{\prime}|s_{cos}(q,q^{\prime})>\epsilon,q^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}_{q}^{K}\right\}.

After obtaining the dynamically filtered nearest neighbors, we design the intent attention network to fuse the embedded knowledge into the search-enhanced query representations:

αq′\displaystyle\alpha_{q^{\prime}} =exp⁡(eqg​r​a​p​h​W​eq′g​r​a​p​h)∑q′′∈𝒩qd​y​nexp⁡(eqg​r​a​p​h​W​eq′′g​r​a​p​h),\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(e_{q}^{graph}\,W\,e_{q^{\prime}}^{graph})}{\sum\nolimits_{q^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{N}_{q}^{dyn}}\exp(e_{q}^{graph}\,W\,e_{q^{\prime\prime}}^{graph})}, (5)
eqs​e​a​r​c​h\displaystyle e_{q}^{search} =∑q′∈𝒩qd​y​nαq′×eq′g​r​a​p​h,\displaystyle=\sum\nolimits_{q^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}_{q}^{dyn}}\;\,\alpha_{q^{\prime}}\,\times\,e_{q^{\prime}}^{graph},

where WW is a learnable matrix to capture the attentive correlation between queries. In this way, the SUIM module can handle diverse query distributions and overlapping intents, producing robust search-enhanced query representations that facilitate effective tool retrieval, even under OOD scenarios.

In practice, the global query pool 𝒬\mathcal{Q} can be dynamically expanded with the oncoming user interactive data, which makes sure that we can progressively tackle the ever-evolving and diverse user queries with such search-based user intent modeling techniques.

4.2.3 Adaptive Knowledge Transfer Module (AdaKT)

The adaptive knowledge transfer module is designed to incorporate the search-enhanced query representation eqs​e​a​r​c​he_{q}^{search} with the detective knowledge hh produced by the tool usage detection tower. We implement the transfer function with the element-wise gating mechanism for the jointly fused query representation: eqj​o​i​n​t=σ⁡(Linear⁡(h))⊗eqs​e​a​r​c​h,e_{q}^{joint}=\sigma\left(\operatorname{Linear(h)}\right)\otimes e_{q}^{search}, where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, and ⊗\otimes is the element-wise product operator. We also provide the empirical study in Section 6.4 about the different choices of the transfer function, demonstrating that this gating mechanism outperforms alternative fusion strategies such as attention, concatenation, and addition.

As shown in Figure 2, with the three core components introduced above (i.e., QC-GCN, SUIM, and AdaKT), we obtain the graph-enhanced query representation eqg​r​a​p​he_{q}^{graph}, the search-enhanced query representation eqs​e​a​r​c​he_{q}^{search}, and the jointly fused query presentation eqj​o​i​n​te_{q}^{joint}. Hence, we normalize these three query representations, add them together, and estimate the matching score estimation with the normalized graph-enhanced tool representation etg​r​a​p​he_{t}^{graph}:

eq\displaystyle e_{q} =eqg​r​a​p​h‖eqg​r​a​p​h‖+eqs​e​a​r​c​h‖eqs​e​a​r​c​h‖+eqj​o​i​n​t‖eqj​o​i​n​t‖,et=etg​r​a​p​h‖etg​r​a​p​h‖,\displaystyle=\frac{e_{q}^{graph}}{\|e_{q}^{graph}\|}+\frac{e_{q}^{search}}{\|e_{q}^{search}\|}+\frac{e_{q}^{joint}}{\|e_{q}^{joint}\|},\;\;e_{t}=\frac{e_{t}^{graph}}{\|e_{t}^{graph}\|}, (6)
s⁡(q,t)=eqT​et,\displaystyle s(q,t)=e_{q}^{T}\,e_{t}, (7)

4.3 Learning Objective

To optimize tool retrieval, we propose a sampled list-wise loss. For each query qq, we construct a candidate tool set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of size MM, containing all golden tools t∈𝒯qt\in\mathcal{T}_{q} and M−|𝒯q|M-|\mathcal{T}_{q}| randomly sampled negatives from the global tool set. We define the ideal and predicted scoring distributions over tools and the sampled list-wise retrieval loss can be written as follows, where 𝕀⁡(⋅)\mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function:

pq,t=𝕀⁡(t∈𝒯q)/∑t′∈𝒮𝕀⁡(t∈𝒯q),t∈𝒮,p_{q,t}={\mathbb{I}(t\in\mathcal{T}_{q})}/{\sum\nolimits_{t^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{I}(t\in\mathcal{T}_{q})},\;\;t\in\mathcal{S}, (8)
p^q,t=exp⁡(s⁡(q,t))/∑t′∈𝒮exp⁡(s⁡(q,t′)),t∈𝒮,\hat{p}_{q,t}={\exp(s(q,t))}/{\sum\nolimits_{t^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}\exp(s(q,t^{\prime}))},\;\;t\in\mathcal{S}, (9)
ℒr​e​t=−∑t∈𝒮pq,tlogp^q,t+(1−pq,t)log(1−p^q,t).\mathcal{L}_{ret}=-\sum\nolimits_{t\in\mathcal{S}}p_{q,t}\log\hat{p}_{q,t}+(1-p_{q,t})\log(1-\hat{p}_{q,t}). (10)

Inspired by [32], we introduce an in-batch contrastive loss using the two query-centric graphs for regularization. For each batch ℬ\mathcal{B}, we extract positive pairs: (eqQ​T,eqQ​S)(e_{q}^{QT},e_{q}^{QS}) for queries and (esQ​T,esQ​S)(e_{s}^{QT},e_{s}^{QS}) for scenes. Here, esQ​Te_{s}^{QT} is computed via average pooling over the tools linked to the scene in the query-tool graph: esQ​T=∑t∈𝒯qetQ​T/|𝒯q|.e_{s}^{QT}=\sum\nolimits_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{q}}e_{t}^{QT}/{|\mathcal{T}_{q}|}. Based on the two pairs of positive representations, we adopt the InfoNCE [6] loss as follows:

ℒc​o​n=−1|ℬ|∑(q,s)∈ℬ(esim⁡(eqQ​S,eqQ​T)/τ∑q′esim⁡(eqQ​S,eq′Q​T)/τ+esim⁡(esQ​S,esQ​T)/τ∑s′esim⁡(esQ​S,es′Q​T)/τ),\mathcal{L}_{con}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{(q,s)\in\mathcal{B}}\left(\frac{e^{\operatorname{sim}(e_{q}^{QS},e_{q}^{QT})/\tau}}{\sum_{q^{\prime}}e^{\operatorname{sim}(e_{q}^{QS},e_{q^{\prime}}^{QT})/\tau}}+\frac{e^{\operatorname{sim}(e_{s}^{QS},e_{s}^{QT})/\tau}}{\sum_{s^{\prime}}e^{\operatorname{sim}(e_{s}^{QS},e_{s^{\prime}}^{QT})/\tau}}\right), (11)

where τ\tau is the temperature hyperparameter, and sim⁡(⋅,⋅)\operatorname{sim}(\cdot,\cdot) is the dot product operation. Our MassTool can be optimized in an end-to-end manner with the learning objective: ℒ=ℒr​e​t+λ​ℒd​e​t+β​ℒc​o​n,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{ret}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{det}+\beta\mathcal{L}_{con}, where λ\lambda and β\beta are the hyperparameters to balance the loss weights.

5 Tool Usage Dataset Construction

Existing datasets [30, 10, 32] fail to support the dual-step training of tool usage detection and tool retrieval. They only contain queries requiring tool invocations, ignoring the crucial step of determining whether the tool invocation is needed for the query. Hence, we construct the first tool usage detection dataset (dubbed ToolDet) based on the Chatbot Arena dataset [50] with the following systematic filtering and verification process:

  • •

    Semantic Filtering. We first adopt Sentence-BERT [33] to estimate the semantic similarity between each target query from the Chatbot Arena dataset and tool-dependent queries from other tool retrieval datasets (e.g., ToolLens [32]). We retain queries with the maximum similarity scores in the range between 0.4 and 0.6 for further verification. Queries in this range are likely to be tool-independent, while not being so obvious that they could be easily classified as tool-independent without detailed inspection. This ensures the high-quality data for tool usage detection.

  • •

    LLM & Human Verification. To ensure the filtered queries are genuinely tool-independent, we employ a proprietary large language model to analyze and verify that the queries could be resolved without invoking external tools. Moreover, we also engaged human annotators to manually review the remaining queries for the final round of verification. After this rigorous filtering process, we compiled 31,229 high-quality tool-independent queries to form the tool usage detection dataset.

ToolDet is dataset-agnostic and can complement existing tool retrieval datasets to enable the foundation for robust dual-step multi-task modeling. The dataset statistic of ToolDet is shown in Table 3, and we have open-sourced the dataset to further benefit the broader research community.

6 Experiments

6.1 Experiment Setup

Datasets. We conduct experiments on three widely adopted multi-tool retrieval datasets: ToolLens [32], ToolBenchG2 [30], and ToolBenchG3 [30]. For MassTool, we use our ToolDet dataset as the complementary part for these datasets to enable the dual-step multi-task training of both tool usage detection and tool retrieval. The detailed dataset statistics can be found in Appendix C.1.

Evaluation Metrics. Following previous works [32, 51, 10], we use the widely adopted Recall@K and NDCG@K as metrics to evaluate the performance of tool retrieval, with K∈{3,5}K\in\{3,5\}.

Baselines. We adopt ANCE [45], TAS-B [8], coCondensor [4] and Contriever [11] as the backbone retrieval models for evaluation. Building upon these backbone models, we select four model-agnostic tool retrieval methods as our baselines: QTA [49] ,MMRR [14] , APIRetriever [30] and COLT [32]. A detailed description of baselines can be referred to in Appendix C.2.

Implementation Details. Due to page limitations, we give implementation details in Appendix C.3.

6.2 Overall Performance

We evaluate the performance of MassTool in comparison to different backbone models and tool retrieval baselines, and report the results in Table 1. We can obtain the following observations:

  • •

    All tool retrieval methods significantly outperform raw backbone models, confirming the importance of tool retrieval fine-tuning for better user intent modeling and tool document understanding.

  • •

    COLT achieves the best performance among all the baseline methods. Built upon semantic learning, COLT further leverages graph neural networks to integrate high-order collaborative knowledge. This enhances the tool representations and results in better performance over semantic-only baselines.

  • •

    Our proposed MassTool outperforms all the baselines across different datasets and backbones, validating its robustness and generalizability. MassTool enables deep user intent mining through the integration of QC-GCN, SUIM, and AdaKT. In this way, we deepen the insights for user intent mining and thereby unleash the superior performance of MassTool for tool retrieval.

6.3 Query Comprehension

In this section, we further validate the capabilities of MassTool in comprehending complex queries and modeling diverse user intents. The tool retrieval datasets we choose are all multi-tool datasets, where each input query would be associated with multiple tools. Therefore, we choose ToolLens and ToolBenchG3 datasets, and divide their testing sets according to the number of golden tools per query, i.e., |𝒯q||\mathcal{T}_{q}|. Note that the greater the number of golden tools required by a query, the more complex the task it likely involves, which in turn reflects more intricate user intent for the query. We evaluate MassTool and the best baseline COLT on these testing subsets w.r.t. different numbers of golden tools per query, and report the results in Figure 3.

Both the performances of MassTool and COLT decrease as the number of golden tools per query increases. This validates the hypothesis that a large number of golden tools generally indicates a more complex query to be resolved. Moreover, MassTool outperforms COLT on all the testing subsets. Moreover, the relative improvement becomes more pronounced as the number of golden tools increases (i.e., the complex level of query). This demonstrates that MassTool can effectively facilitate the understanding of complex queries and thereby improve the tool retrieval performance with enhanced query representations.

6.4 Transfer Function

In this section, we analyze the different choices of transfer function in the adaptive knowledge transfer module (AdaKT). In addition to the element-wise gating mechanism in our MassTool, given the inputs of detective knowledge hh and search-enhanced query representation eqs​e​a​r​c​he_{q}^{search}, we provide three alternative transfer functions: Attention, Concatenation and Addition. Further details of transfer functions are available in Appendix B.2.

We report the performance of different transfer functions in Table 2. The gating transfer function adopted by our MassTool generally achieves the best performance, except for a few cases. We argue that the design of gating mechanism is more aligned with the dual-step sequential decision-making nature for tool usage detection and tool retrieval. Based on the detective knowledge hh containing the potential information about whether the query should invoke tools or not, we can adaptively conduct element-wise gating for the search-based query representation eqs​e​a​r​c​he_{q}^{search}. In this way, we can selectively filter the unnecessary information and dynamically control the information flow for final prediction, leading to better knowledge fusion for multi-task modeling.

6.5 In-Depth Analysis

We analyze the impact of different components in MassTool, i.e., ablation study. We conduct experiments with four backbone models on ToolLens and ToolBenchG3 datasets. We conduct the ablation study by evaluating the performance of the following model variants: MassTool w/o AdaKT, MassTool w/o SUIM, MassTool w/o DF (Dynamic Filtering), and MassTool w/o CL (Contrastive Learning). Further details of model variants are available in Appendix C.4. We report results in Figure 4 and draw the following observations:

  • •

    MassTool w/o AdaKT suffers from a considerable performance decrease, demonstrating the importance of casting the dual-step multi-task modeling of both tool usage detection and tool retrieval tasks. The information gained from the previous detective stage can establish a more comprehensive view of user queries and intents, thereby leading to better retrieval performance.

  • •

    MassTool w/o SUIM and w/o DF generally meet significant performance drops, validating the effectiveness of our search-based techniques to model the nuanced user intents.

  • •

    The performance of MassTool w/o CL also declines to some extent. This shows the importance of regularization to better learn the query-tool-scene representations with multiple views, preventing the neural tool retriever from overfitting.

Due to the page limitation, we provide more analysis experiments in Appendix D, covering the hyperparameter studies and visualization of query representations, respectively.

7 Conclusion and Limitation

In this paper, we focus on tool retrieval for large language models (LLMs). We identify key challenges of query representation optimization, particularly in capturing nuanced user intent and addressing the dual-step sequential decision-making nature of tool retrieval. To this end, we propose a multi-task search-based tool retrieval framework (i.e., MassTool), featuring a two-tower architecture to enable the dual-step training of both tool usage detection and tool retrieval tasks. Moreover, we release the first tool usage detection dataset (i.e., ToolDet), which can be integrated with existing tool retrieval datasets for enhancements. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of MassTool in enhancing query representations and improving tool retrieval performance. While effective, MassTool does not yet support continual tool expansion and does not interact with tool-augmented LLMs. As for future work, we will explore the synergy between tool-augmented LLMs and external tools with the tool retriever as the bridge.

Appendix A Broader Impact

Our work contributes to improving the quality of tool use in large language models and lays a foundation for enhancing the fundamental tool-use capabilities of large language models, especially when facing the web-scale massive amount of tools available for complex user queries. However, the training data required may involve personal information, potentially raising concerns about privacy and security.

Appendix B Methodology Details

B.1 LightGCN Operations for QC-GCN

We give the detailed computational process of applying LightGCN within QC-GCN to obtain the final graph representations, as introduced in Section 4.2.1. Here, we take the query-tool graph as an example, while the operations on the query-scene graph are the same.

Specifically, we pass the query qq and tool tt through the pretrained language model (PLM) to get the initial query and tool embeddings, and further obtain the scene embeddings via the average pooling over tool embeddings from the golden tool set 𝒯q\mathcal{T}_{q}:

eq0=PLM(q),et0=PLM(t),es0=1|𝒯q|∑t∈𝒯qet0.\displaystyle e_{q}^{0}=\operatorname{PLM}(q),\;\;e_{t}^{0}=\operatorname{PLM}(t),\;\;e_{s}^{0}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{q}|}\sum\nolimits_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{q}}e_{t}^{0}. (12)

Then, we apply multi-layer message propagation on the two graphs. Since the operations for the two graphs are symmetric, we take the query-tool graph as an example, and similar operations can be conducted for the query-scene graph. At the ll-th layer for the query-tool graph, the message propagation can be written as:

eql=∑t∈𝒩qetl−1|𝒩q|​|𝒩t|,etl=∑q∈𝒩teql−1|𝒩q|​|𝒩t|,l=1,…,L,\displaystyle e_{q}^{l}=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{N}_{q}}\frac{e_{t}^{l-1}}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{N}_{q}|}\sqrt{|\mathcal{N}_{t}|}},\;e_{t}^{l}=\sum_{q\in\mathcal{N}_{t}}\frac{e_{q}^{l-1}}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{N}_{q}|}\sqrt{|\mathcal{N}_{t}|}},\,l=1,\dots,L, (13)

where 𝒩q\mathcal{N}_{q} and 𝒩t\mathcal{N}_{t} are the neighbor sets for query qq and tool tt, respectively. Next, we sum up the outputs from each layer to obtain the final representations for the query-tool graph:

eqQ​T=∑l=0Leql,etQ​T=∑l=0Letl.e_{q}^{QT}=\sum\nolimits_{l=0}^{L}e_{q}^{l},\;\;e_{t}^{QT}=\sum\nolimits_{l=0}^{L}e_{t}^{l}. (14)

B.2 Transfer Function Variants

we provide the following alternative transfer functions in addition to the element-wise gating mechanism in MassTool:

  • •

    Attention. We apply self-attention [42] over hh and eqs​e​a​r​c​he_{q}^{search}, and perform element-wise addition to fuse attentive output vectors.

  • •

    Concatenation. We concatenate hh and eqs​e​a​r​c​he_{q}^{search}, and feed them to a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) for implicit knowledge fusion.

  • •

    Addition. We conduct element-wise addition for hh and eqs​e​a​r​c​he_{q}^{search}. This transfer function is simple but not learnable.

Appendix C Experiment Setup Details

C.1 Datasets Statistics

We give the detailed dataset statistics in Table 3, including the three benchmarking datasets and our developed ToolDet dataset. Datasets are split into training and testing sets with a ratio of 9:1.

C.2 Baselines

We select four model-agnostic tool retrieval methods as our baselines:

  • •

    QTA [49] uses LLMs to rewrite user queries to further enrich the training data for tool retrievers.

  • •

    MMRR [14] employs LLMs to generate synthetic tool descriptions based on the user input query, and then retrieves similar tools from the global pool.

  • •

    APIRetriever [30] finetunes the neural retriever with refined query logs and tool documents.

  • •

    COLT [32] designs cross-view graph learning for better collaborative patterns among tools.

C.3 Implementation Details

We utilize the BEIR [41] framework to implement dense retrieval backbone models. We freeze the dense retrieval backbone models during the training of MassTool. We adopt Adam optimizer with a batch size of 2048, and select the learning rate from the set {1e-3, 5e–3, 1e–4, 5e–4, 1e–5}. For SUIM, the number of neighbors KK is chosen from {10,20,25,30,35,40}\{10,20,25,30,35,40\}, and the threshold ϵ\epsilon for dynamic filtering is selected from {0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0}\{0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0\}. We set the contrastive loss weight β\beta as 0.040.04, and select the tool usage detection loss weight λ\lambda from {0.08,0.2,0.5,1.0}\{0.08,0.2,0.5,1.0\}. For fair comparison, we finetune all the baselines to achieve their best performance.

C.4 Ablation settings

We conduct the ablation study by evaluating the performance of the following model variants:

  • •

    MassTool. The complete version of our proposed framework.

  • •

    MassTool w/o AdaKT. We remove the adaptive knowledge transfer module, resulting in single-tower learning for tool retrieval task without tool usage detection.

  • •

    MassTool w/o SUIM. We remove the search-based user intent modeling, and AdaKT directly takes as input the graph-enhanced query representation instead of the search-enhanced one.

  • •

    MassTool w/o DF. We remove the dynamic filtering mechanism (DF) in SUIM, and therefore the number of nearest neighbors for every input query stays the same, i.e., KK.

  • •

    MassTool w/o CL. We remove the contrastive loss in Eq. 11.

Appendix D Additional Experiments

D.1 Hyperparameter Study

Tool usage detection loss weight λ\lambda.

We select the weight of tool usage detection loss λ\lambda from {0.08, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0}, and report the results in Figure 5. We can observe that MassTool generally favors a relatively small loss weight for tool usage detection, compared with the tool retrieval loss weight which is set to 1. The binary tool usage detection task is significantly simpler than the tool retrieval task. Therefore, we need to assign a smaller loss weight to the detection task to slow down its learning pace. This ensures that the learning progress and convergence speed of two towers in the MassTool model remain synchronized, preventing the tool usage detection tower from overfitting prematurely.

Threshold ϵ\epsilon for dynamic filtering.

We study the impact of the threshold ϵ\epsilon for dynamic filtering in SUIM. We select the threshold ϵ\epsilon from {0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0}\{0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0\} and report the results on ToolLens and ToolBenchG3 datasets in Figure 6. Note that ϵ=1.0\epsilon=1.0 means that we remove the dynamic filtering and accept all the top-KK nearest neighbors. We observe that the optimal value for threshold generally lies in the range of [0.7,0.9][0.7,0.9], indicating the importance of eliminating potential noisy neighbor queries.

D.2 Query Representation Visualization

To showcase the capability of MassTool in modeling multi-aspect information of input queries for tool retrieval, we visualize the different sets of query representations in MassTool using the t-SNE projection [24]. Specifically, we visualize the following three different types of query representations based on the Contriever backbone model on ToolLens and ToolBenchG3 datasets:

  • •

    Graph-enhanced query representations eqg​r​a​p​he_{q}^{graph} from query-centric graph convolution network (QC-GCN).

  • •

    Search-enhanced query representations eqs​e​a​r​c​he_{q}^{search} from search-based user intent modeling (SUIM).

  • •

    Jointly fused query representations eqj​o​i​n​te_{q}^{joint} from adaptive knowledge transfer module (AdaKT).

We uniformly sample 300 queries from the tool retrieval dataset 𝒟r​e​t\mathcal{D}_{ret}, and show the visualization in Figure 7. We can observe that graph-enhanced query representations (in green) generally cast a uniform distribution, while the search-enhanced (in blue) and jointly fused (in yellow) query representations show more compact but different distributional manifolds within the query embedding space. We argue that QC-GCN is designed to capture overall and basic user intents based on the query-tool-scene collaborative patterns, and SUIM and AdaKT further refine and specify on more diverse, rare and nuanced aspects of the input query. As a result, we can deeply explore the underlying user intent and thereby optimize the query representations for better tool retrieval performance.
